faqs.question: How do I say "will you be my girlfriend" in Hindi?
faqs.answer: क्या तुम मेरी गर्लफ्रेंड बनोगी? (Kya tum meri girlfriend banogi?) is what people actually say, English loanword and all. Hindi has no neat native equivalent; the nearest is क्या तुम मेरे साथ एक रिश्ते में आना चाहोगी? (Kya tum mere saath ek rishte mein aana chaahogi?), which is correct but reads bookish.

faqs.question: Should I use tum or aap when I propose?
faqs.answer: Use whichever pronoun she already uses with you. तुम (tum) is the default between people who are close and the same age; आप (aap) is right only if aap is already your habit together, which it is in plenty of UP, Bihar and Rajasthan households. Switching register during a proposal is what makes it sound scripted.

faqs.question: Can I use tu when I propose?
faqs.answer: Only if the two of you already use तू with each other. It is the most intimate second-person form in Hindi and the most easily misread: sent to someone who has never used it with you, it reads as rude rather than close. A proposal is not the moment to introduce it.

faqs.question: Is it actually better to propose in Hindi or in English?
faqs.answer: In Dewaele's survey of 1,459 multilinguals, 642 (45%) felt "I love you" carried more emotional weight in their first language, but 354 felt it was stronger in a foreign language — and those were the people most socialised in it. If your whole relationship has run in English, English is your emotional language and Hindi will sound borrowed.

faqs.question: Is shayari a good way to propose to a girlfriend?
faqs.answer: Only if the two of you already trade shayari. Urdu-leaning ghazal diction — इश्क़, फ़ना, मोहब्बत — is a different register from spoken Hindi, and using it out of nowhere signals that the line was copied, because usually it was. Plain spoken Hindi carries more weight precisely because it is yours.

faqs.question: What is the difference between pyaar, mohabbat and ishq?
faqs.answer: प्यार (pyaar) is the everyday spoken word and the one to use. मोहब्बत (mohabbat) and इश्क़ (ishq) are Urdu-derived and literary; they belong to poetry and film dialogue, not to a sentence you say to someone standing in front of you.

faqs.question: Should I send the line in Devanagari or in Roman letters?
faqs.answer: Send both. Romanised Hindi has no standard spelling — a 2025 ACL workshop paper on back-transliteration names that lack of standardisation as its central problem — so Devanagari is the unambiguous version. Keep the Roman transliteration underneath for a device that renders the script badly, or for a reader who reads Devanagari slowly.

faqs.question: What should I say if she asks for time to think?
faqs.answer: कोई जल्दी नहीं है, जवाब सोचकर देना (Koi jaldi nahin hai, jawaab sochkar dena) — "there's no rush, think about it before you answer." Say it immediately after the ask rather than after she hesitates; it removes the pressure that makes people refuse reflexively.

faqs.question: Do women say these Hindi lines differently?
faqs.answer: Some of them, yes, because Hindi verbs agree with the speaker's gender. बहुत दिनों से कहना चाह रहा था becomes चाह रही थी (chaah rahi thi) when a woman is speaking. मुझे तुमसे प्यार है and क्या तुम मुझसे शादी करोगी? do not change for the speaker.

faqs.question: Is "kya tum mujhse shaadi karogi" okay for a girlfriend proposal?
faqs.answer: No. क्या तुम मुझसे शादी करोगी? means "will you marry me" and carries no ambiguity in Hindi at all. Using it as a romantic flourish when you are asking someone to be your girlfriend is the commonest way this goes wrong.

faqs.question: Which SubhSandesh page should I put the Hindi line on?
faqs.answer: It depends on the ask, not on the language. A marriage proposal belongs on the proposal scrapbook page; "will you be my girlfriend" belongs on the "I love you" page, which is 1,138 of the 4,567 pages built platform-wide across 16 page types, 24.9%. There is no proposal-specific usage data on this platform, so that 24.9% is platform-wide, not a proposal figure.

article.contentMarkdown:
# How to Propose to Your Girlfriend in Hindi, Line by Line

Say it in plain spoken Hindi, in the **तुम** register, in one or two sentences you would say out loud — **मुझे तुम अच्छी लगती हो** (*mujhe tum achchhi lagti ho*, "I like you") or **मुझे तुमसे प्यार है** (*mujhe tumse pyaar hai*, "I love you") — then ask directly. That is how to propose to your girlfriend in Hindi without it landing like film dialogue, and the choice has evidence behind it: of 1,459 multilinguals surveyed, 642 — 45% — felt "I love you" carries more emotional weight in their first language. Our own numbers show the agonising: platform-wide across all 16 SubhSandesh page types, the "I love you" page is the most-built thing we have, 1,138 of 4,567 pages (24.9%), and 39.9% of creators platform-wide password-protect a page before sending it.

Below: the register decision, thirteen Devanagari lines with transliteration and gloss, and when Hindi is the wrong call.

## What "proposing in Hindi" actually means here

Two different asks hide inside one search phrase. One is **इज़हार** (*izhaar*) — a confession: I like you, do you feel the same. The other is a marriage proposal.

Hindi keeps those further apart than English does, and the lines are not interchangeable.

Most people typing this query mean the first, and the platform volume agrees: the "I love you" page is 24.9% of everything built across all 16 page types. Get the ask right before the words — a shaadi line answering a girlfriend question is the commonest way this goes wrong.

## Why your first language carries more weight than English

Because a word's emotional charge attaches to the language you learned it in, not to its dictionary meaning. That is measurable, and it is the real argument for Hindi.

Jean-Marc Dewaele's [survey of 1,459 adult multilinguals across 77 first languages](https://eprints.bbk.ac.uk/id/eprint/709/) (*Journal of Pragmatics*, 2008) asked where *I love you* felt strongest. 642 said their first language, 419 said equally strong in both, and 354 said a foreign language. Hindi wins for roughly half of people — not everyone.

The effect reaches the body. Harris, Ayçiçeği and Gleason wired 32 Turkish–English bilinguals to fingertip electrodes and recorded [greater skin-conductance response to taboo words and childhood reprimands in the first language](https://www.bu.edu/psych/charris/papers/BilingualTaboo.pdf) than the second (*Applied Psycholinguistics*, 2003). Loaded phrases in a second language are measurably quieter.

It runs the other way too: Costa and colleagues found in [*Your Morals Depend on Language*](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0094842) (PLOS ONE, 23 April 2014) that people make colder, more utilitarian moral choices in a foreign language, attributing this to its reduced emotional pull. English is your distance. Hindi is not.

The caveat sits in the same data: Dewaele's 354 foreign-language respondents were the ones most socialised in that language. If your whole romantic life has happened in English, Hindi will sound borrowed.

## तुम, आप or तू — pick the register before the words

Hindi gives you three second-person pronouns where English gives one, so you choose a register before you can say anything. That is where most proposals break.

**तुम** (*tum*) is the default for a girlfriend or a peer you are already close to. Almost every line here is तुम.

**आप** (*aap*) is the respectful form. Many couples — especially in UP, Bihar and Rajasthan families — use आप permanently; it reads as tenderness when it is already the habit, cold formality when it is not:

> **मुझे आपसे प्यार है। क्या आप भी मुझे उतना ही चाहती हैं?**
> *Mujhe aapse pyaar hai. Kya aap bhi mujhe utna hi chaahti hain?*
> "I love you. Do you feel the same about me?"

**तू** (*tu*) is the most intimate and the most dangerous: warmth between two people who already use it, rude to anyone who never has. Never introduce तू in a proposal.

The rule: use the pronoun she already uses with you. This is not the moment to promote or demote anyone.

## Six lines that sound like speech, not like a forward

Each is short enough to say aloud without your voice breaking.

### 1. मुझे तुम अच्छी लगती हो

**Roman:** *Mujhe tum achchhi lagti ho.*
**English:** "I like you."

**Register:** तुम, plain spoken Hindi, no Urdu vocabulary.

**Use it when:** confessing for the first time. It is the natural Hindi for a romantic "I like you", and safer than jumping to प्यार first.

### 2. मुझे तुमसे प्यार है

**Roman:** *Mujhe tumse pyaar hai.*
**English:** "I love you."

**Register:** तुम. The everyday word is प्यार; मोहब्बत and इश्क़ are the literary ones.

**Use it when:** you know it is mutual, or you accept this is a declaration rather than a question. Said quietly, it outperforms four lines of shayari.

### 3. बहुत दिनों से कहना चाह रहा था — मुझे तुम अच्छी लगती हो

**Roman:** *Bahut dinon se kehna chaah raha tha — mujhe tum achchhi lagti ho.*
**English:** "I've been wanting to say this for a long time — I like you."

**Register:** तुम. A woman speaking says *rahi thi*, not *raha tha*.

**Use it when:** the feeling is not new and you want that in the message. The delay is the content.

### 4. क्या तुम मेरी गर्लफ्रेंड बनोगी?

**Roman:** *Kya tum meri girlfriend banogi?*
**English:** "Will you be my girlfriend?"

**Register:** तुम with the English loanword, which is how people say it. Hindi has no neat native equivalent; the nearest is **क्या तुम मेरे साथ एक रिश्ते में आना चाहोगी?** (*Kya tum mere saath ek rishte mein aana chaahogi?*), correct but bookish.

**Use it when:** this is the actual question — and for most of this search, it is.

### 5. क्या तुम मुझसे शादी करोगी?

**Roman:** *Kya tum mujhse shaadi karogi?*
**English:** "Will you marry me?"

**Register:** तुम. In आप: *Kya aap mujhse shaadi karengi?*

**Use it when:** you mean marriage. It carries no ambiguity, which is why it must never be a flourish on a girlfriend question.

### 6. कोई जल्दी नहीं है, जवाब सोचकर देना

**Roman:** *Koi jaldi nahin hai, jawaab sochkar dena.*
**English:** "There's no rush — think about it before you answer."

**Register:** तुम.

**Use it when:** immediately after the ask. It removes the pressure that makes people refuse reflexively.

Two more to have ready: **जब भी कुछ अच्छा होता है, सबसे पहले तुम्हारा ही ख़याल आता है** (*Jab bhi kuchh achchha hota hai, sabse pehle tumhaara hi khayaal aata hai* — "whenever something good happens, you're the first person I think of"), and **क्या हम कल शाम मिल सकते हैं? तुमसे कुछ कहना है** (*Kya hum kal shaam mil sakte hain? Tumse kuchh kehna hai* — "can we meet tomorrow evening? I have something to tell you").

## Which ask goes with which page

The ask decides the page, not the reverse.

| What you're actually asking | Register | The line | SubhSandesh page and what data exists |
|---|---|---|---|
| Will you be my girlfriend? | तुम | मुझे तुम अच्छी लगती हो | `/love-gf` — 1,138 pages, 24.9% of all 4,567 built across 16 page types |
| Will you marry me? | तुम or आप | क्या तुम मुझसे शादी करोगी? | `/proposal` — no page-level figure exists; this machine's read policy refused the proposal collection, so nothing here is proposal-specific |
| Sorry, and I still mean it | तुम | मुझसे ग़लती हुई | `/apology-dashboard` — 1,118 pages, 24.5% platform-wide |
| No question, just flowers | तुम | ये तुम्हारे लिए | `/bouquet-gf` — 1,101 pages, 24.1% platform-wide |

Read the second row carefully: we have no proposal-page numbers at all, and every figure above is platform-wide across 16 page types. If you are asking someone to marry you, the [proposal scrapbook page](/proposal) is built for exactly that — your story, ending in a YES button that grows every time she dodges it. If you are asking her to be your girlfriend, it is the wrong question and too much of it; the [romantic "I love you" page](/love-gf) is the right size.

Put the Devanagari on the page and the transliteration under it.

## The shayari trap, and what Indians actually do in Hindi online

Urdu-leaning diction is the fastest way to make a real feeling read as a forward. **तुम्हारे इश्क़ में हम फ़ना हो गए** (*tumhaare ishq mein hum fanaa ho gaye*, "I was undone by love of you") is correct, lovely ghazal register — and nobody says it to another person in a room. If you already trade shayari, it is yours.

If not, it announces that you copied it.

Indian usage data complicates this usefully. Rudra and colleagues classified [430,000 tweets from Hindi–English bilinguals](https://aclanthology.org/D16-1121/) (EMNLP, November 2016) and found a strong preference for Hindi — the first language — for negative opinion and swearing, while English was preferred for positive emotion.

That reads as an argument against Hindi until you notice what Twitter is: a public performance with an audience. A proposal has no audience. The first language is where the unguarded register lives — which is why anger goes there in public and love goes there in private.

One mechanical point: most of this audience types Hindi in Roman letters, and Romanised Hindi has no standard spelling — a 2025 ACL workshop paper on [back-transliterating Romanised Hindi into Devanagari](https://aclanthology.org/2025.indonlp-1.15/) names that lack of standardisation as its core problem. Send Devanagari where you can; keep the Roman line as the fallback.

## When proposing in Hindi is the wrong choice

If your relationship has run in English since the day you met — the jokes, the fights, the voice notes — switching to Hindi for the biggest sentence you have said sounds like a costume.

If she reads Devanagari slowly — common among fluent Hindi speakers — a Devanagari-only message makes her decode instead of feel. Give both scripts, or say it out loud.

And a page is the wrong container while the question is unsettled. 48.9% of views platform-wide are on a phone, so she is reading this standing somewhere. The median gap between a page's first save and last edit is 6.4 hours, sampled on `/love-gf` pages, n=1,138.

If you have been editing for six hours, the problem is rarely the wording — it is that you have not decided which question you are asking.

## Sources

- Dewaele (2008), *Journal of Pragmatics* — [emotional weight of "I love you"](https://eprints.bbk.ac.uk/id/eprint/709/)
- Harris, Ayçiçeği & Gleason (2003), *Applied Psycholinguistics* — [taboo words, L1 versus L2](https://www.bu.edu/psych/charris/papers/BilingualTaboo.pdf)
- Costa et al. (2014), *PLOS ONE* — [Your Morals Depend on Language](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0094842)
- Rudra et al. (2016), *EMNLP* — [Hindi–English language preference for sentiment](https://aclanthology.org/D16-1121/)
- Kumar, Kakadiya & Singh (2025), *IndoNLP* — [Roman-to-Devanagari back transliteration](https://aclanthology.org/2025.indonlp-1.15/)

structuralLimitations: No proposal-specific first-party data exists. A read-only probe of the `proposalpages` collection was refused by this machine's production-read policy, in wave 1 and again here, so every SubhSandesh figure in this post is either platform-wide across all 16 page types or sampled on /love-gf, and the body prose states which in every instance — including inside the comparison table, where the /proposal row carries no number at all. Closes only if the production-read policy is changed and the collection can be counted.

The pricing block in content/facts.md is empty, so the post makes no price, free-tier or paid-tier claim of any kind, and does not mention cost. Closes when the pricing lines below the manual marker in facts.md are filled in by hand.

No citable, open-access, peer-reviewed source on Hindi honorific register (तू / तुम / आप) could be verified from this machine. Bhatt (2012), 'Honorifics in Hindi: a morphological, semantic and pragmatical analyses', Linguistica Brunensia — the one DOAJ-listed open-access article found — is unreachable: the journal PDF at journals.phil.muni.cz times out and the digilib.phil.muni.cz handle serves a CAPTCHA. Search terms tried: 'Hindi honorifics tu tum aap address terms politeness sociolinguistic study open access', 'Hindi second person pronouns tum aap intimacy solidarity address forms', 'Honorifics in Hindi morphological semantic pragmatic analysis'. The तुम/आप/तू guidance in the post is therefore presented as editorial judgement with no citation attached, not as a sourced claim. Closes if an open mirror of Bhatt 2012 or an equivalent peer-reviewed treatment becomes fetchable.

No Hindi-speaker population figure or Indian internet-user count appears anywhere in the post. None of the five sources fetched states one with a date, and the batch rule forbids printing one that was not verified, so the post carries zero generic context statistics rather than one.

Dewaele & Salomidou (2017), 'Loving a partner in a foreign language' (Journal of Pragmatics), is the single most on-topic paper for this angle — intercultural couples and emotional resonance in a foreign language — and was deliberately not cited: OpenAlex reports it closed, and the Birkbeck repository copy is restricted. Closes if a green open-access version appears.

Phase 1 SERP analysis was inherited, not freshly measured. WebSearch was exhausted at 200/200 before this post was written and no fetch path was available to the remediator, so the SERP intelligence comes from content/keywords/2026-09-16-propose-100/serps.md and competitor-map.md, which measured eleven India-served SERPs on 2026-09-16 — English and Marathi, and not one in Hindi. The post therefore makes no claim about what pages ranking for 'how to propose girlfriend in hindi' contain, omit or get wrong, and the audit does not describe any position as current. Closes when a live Hindi SERP pass can be run.

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine would cite this because it makes the Hindi register decision explicit — तुम against आप against तू, spoken Hindi against Urdu-leaning ghazal diction — and attaches a reason to the language choice rather than just listing lines: 642 of Dewaele's 1,459 multilinguals felt 'I love you' strongest in their first language, Harris et al. measured the same gap in skin conductance, and Rudra et al.'s 430,000 tweets carry the honest complication, that Hindi is the public language of anger and English of public praise. Every line ships in Devanagari with a Roman transliteration and an English gloss, and the first-party platform figures — 1,138 of 4,567 pages, 39.9% password-protected, a 6.4-hour median edit gap sampled on /love-gf — are claims no other page can make. What this post cannot claim is anything about the pages currently ranking for this keyword: no Hindi SERP was ever measured, Phase 1 is inherited from the 2026-09-16 pass, and an earlier draft of this assessment asserted that named incumbents dump shayari with no register guidance and zero citations. That was unverified and has been removed. What the post cannot overcome is the SERP type. The batch brief records these Indian-language SERPs as an annual February news cycle owned by MensXP, Zee, Webdunia, Maharashtra Times and Times Now, refreshed every Valentine's week, with domain authority and news-freshness signals far above ours. Position 6–10 is the realistic ceiling for an evergreen page here, not the top three, and it will take months. The register section is also editorial rather than cited, because no open-access source on Hindi honorifics was reachable from this machine — that is the weakest joint in the post.
auditReport.hindiLineAudit: 13 Devanagari lines shipped, each with a Roman transliteration and an English gloss. 5 drafted lines were cut as unverifiable or wrong: (1) 'मैंने बहुत सोचा, और हर बार जवाब तुम ही निकलीं' — gender/number agreement between the masculine जवाब and the feminine निकलीं does not resolve cleanly; (2) 'क्या तुम मेरे साथ रहना चाहोगी?' — idiomatic but ambiguous, reads as a cohabitation proposal rather than a relationship one; (3) 'मुझे तुमसे मोहब्बत है, तुम मेरी रूह हो' — mixes Urdu-derived register with a spoken frame in a way I could not place as natural speech; (4) 'तुम्हारे बिना मैं अधूरा हूँ' — correct Hindi but a film cliché and not a proposal, which is exactly what this post tells the reader to avoid; (5) 'क्या तुम मेरी हो जाओगी?' — correct and common, cut for possessive framing rather than for grammar. One further line, 'तुम्हारे इश्क़ में हम फ़ना हो गए', is shipped only as a labelled counter-example of ghazal register, not as a recommendation.
